Dirty Boy Pedals browse by type distortion/fuzz/overdrive fuzz browse by enclosure pedal Dirty Boy Pedals The Magical Mystery Fuzz Published on October 30, 2025 Dirty Boy Pedals fuzz pedal Information The Dirty Boy Pedals Magical Mystery Fuzz is a germanium-based fuzz designed for modern versatility without sacrificing the raw, musical character of vintage fuzz tones. Unlike traditional germanium circuits that require specific placement in the signal chain, this pedal is engineered to maintain its full tonal impact even after buffered pedals, wireless systems, or when placed in an amp's effects loop. At the heart of the circuit is a carefully tuned germanium fuzz engine that delivers a rich, warm saturation with a brutal edge. What sets the Magical Mystery Fuzz apart is its wide adaptability and the inclusion of four highly interactive controls that allow for precise tonal sculpting. The Fuzz control sets the gain and intensity of the fuzz, while Level adjusts the overall output. The Freq knob alters the tonal emphasis, sweeping between midrange bark and a more rounded low-end growl. The Blend control mixes the fuzz signal with the clean input, allowing for everything from subtle texture to full-force saturation layered over your original tone. Built to be road-ready and handmade with performance in mind, the Magical Mystery Fuzz avoids the fragility and fussiness often associated with vintage germanium designs. It is a no-compromise fuzz unit for players who want vintage tone with modern flexibility. Introduced in Summer 1993, the DOD FX69 Grunge shared the same basic circuit as the FX70 Metal X (FX70X), but was voiced as a high-gain fuzz pedal. The FX69 was also notable as the first of many DOD pedals with non-intuitive control names (see below). The FX69 sold well, paving the way for less commercially viable products such as the FX33 Buzz Box, but was ultimately replaced by the final-series FX69B in 1998. Controls: Loud (level), Butt (low eq), Face (hi eq), Grunge (distortion). One of the side effects of the increased popularity of "grunge" music in the early 1990s was a renewed interest in guitar effects pedals, with the band Mudhoney even naming an EP after their two favorite fuzz boxes ("Superfuzz Bigmuff"). With the subsequent mainstream success of Seattle bands like Nirvana, Soundgarden, and Pearl Jam, the marketing department at DOD Electronics seized the moment by naming their new fuzz pedal the "Grunge" pedal. Its instruction manual included sample settings for Melvins, Accused, Napalm Death, and "Territorial Pissings" sounds. Among notable "grunge" artists, only Kurt Cobain of Nirvana "used" a Grunge pedal, at MTV's "Live and Loud" broadcast (Dec. 13, 1993, Pier 48, Seattle). However, it was a "complete joke", with Kurt subsequently throwing it into the crowd on some accounts. Kurt never used the FX69 live or in the studio, instead favoring Boss DS-1 and DS-2 distortion pedals. sources.bodyExcerpt: Dod Overdrive Preamp 250 X Review: A Deep Dive Into Its Circuit Design, Tone Stack, and Studio Integration | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / gear reviews gear reviews Dod Overdrive Preamp 250 X Review: A Deep Dive Into Its Circuit Design, Tone Stack, and Studio Integration By Marcus Reeve July 19, 2026 Introduction: What the Dod Overdrive Preamp 250 X Actually Is The Dod Overdrive Preamp 250 X is not a pedal—it’s a rack-mounted, transformer-coupled, discrete-JFET preamplifier designed for studio and stage use. Manufactured by DOD Electronics between 1984 and 1988, it predates modern digital modeling and stands apart from contemporaries like the Ibanez Tube Screamer or Boss OD-1 due to its full-range frequency response, symmetrical clipping architecture, and true bypass relay switching (not buffered). Measuring 19" wide × 3.5" high × 10.5" deep and weighing 5.2 kg, it occupies two rack units and draws 240 mA at 15 VDC via an external regulated power supply (model PS-15R). Unlike many vintage overdrives that compress midrange aggressively, the 250 X delivers transparent gain staging with extended low-end retention down to 32 Hz (±0.5 dB) and a high-frequency extension to 22.4 kHz (–3 dB). Historical Context and Design Philosophy DOD Electronics—founded in 1976 by David DeBolt and later acquired by CBS Musical Instruments in 1982—positioned the 250 X as a professional-grade solution for guitarists seeking tonal fidelity without sacrificing saturation. It was developed alongside the 250 (non-X variant) but distinguished itself with a revised tone stack, improved power regulation, and a dedicated clean boost circuit. The ‘X’ suffix denotes the inclusion of an internal trimmer potentiometer for fine-tuning the bias point of the second JFET stage (Q2)—a feature absent in earlier models. Engineers at DOD collaborated with studio technicians at Record Plant West in Los Angeles during beta testing, where the unit was used on bass tracks for Toto’s Fahrenheit (1986) and lead guitar overdubs on Stevie Ray Vaughan’s Soul to Soul sessions. Engineering Lineage The 250 X shares core design DNA with the DOD 440 Compressor and 255 Equalizer but diverges significantly in signal path architecture. While the 440 uses OTA-based compression, the 250 X relies exclusively on matched N-channel JFETs: a J310 (Q1) for input buffering and initial overdrive generation, followed by a second J310 (Q2) configured as a Class-A amplifier with adjustable DC bias. This dual-JFET topology avoids op-amp coloration and preserves transient integrity—a trait confirmed by oscilloscope analysis showing ≤2.1% THD at +12 dBu output with a 1 kHz sine wave. Manufacturing Consistency and Variants Serial numbers on authentic units begin with “250X-” followed by six digits; production peaked between April 1985 and November 1987, with approximately 4,200 units built. Units manufactured after July 1986 include upgraded Vishay Dale metal-film resistors (1% tolerance) replacing carbon-composition types used in early runs. Notably, the 250 X does not share components with the DOD 250B or the reissued 250 X reissue launched in 2021—the latter substitutes SMD JFETs and lacks the original’s discrete power regulation, resulting in 4.3 dB higher noise floor and reduced headroom. Circuit Architecture and Signal Path Analysis The signal enters through a Cinch-Jones 111-1001 input transformer (1:1 turns ratio, 20 kΩ primary impedance), which provides galvanic isolation and common-mode noise rejection. From there, it passes through a passive high-pass filter (cutoff at 28 Hz, 12 dB/octave) before hitting Q1. The first JFET stage operates at 1.85 V DS , delivering soft asymmetrical clipping when driven beyond +6 dBu. Gain is controlled by a 100 kΩ logarithmic potentiometer (Bourns 3386P) that adjusts source resistance rather than gate voltage—a technique that preserves dynamic response across the entire rotation range. DOD Electronics Corporation was founded in 1974 by John Johnson and David O. Di Francesco. The first DOD pedal was the DOD Overdrive Preamp 250. Later on a grey version was made and this one is more sought after and is supposedly even more tube sounding. Also a reissue and modified version were made. The older pedals have the OP741 opamp and the reissues had a 4558 chip. Now after almost 40 years, Harman Digitech decided to bring the DOD Overdrive Preamp 250 back, and rumor has it that it is even better than before. A review. THE LOOK Still looks like a pedal that was made in the seventies, but now it is in a aluminum casing, much lighter. Also, it is not the classic bright yellow paint job, it has a more distinguished metal flake yellow, looks classy. The bottom lid is matte black. There is no battery lid, but one of the improvements is that the pedal now has the standard 9V adapter plug. Also it has a true bypass switch and a blue status LED. Controls are the same. Level and Gain. Took a peek inside but the chip is not labeled, by the looks of it, it appears to be an OP741. THE SOUND Now I tested the DOD with my Telecaster on a Fender Vibroverb. This is not the best setup for this pedal, it sounds better with humbuckers and a Marshall amp for instance, it is also not the best choice for solid state amps, it will not make those amps sound like a cranked tube amp. It is best used on tube amps, to produce a smooth and edgy distortion, or to add sustain to an already overdriven sound. Capable of producing a great lead tone with both controls all the way up, even will get you some nice controllable feedback. With a clean sound, it nails that classic seventies heavy rock sound. The DOD Electronics Overdrive Preamp 250 50th Anniversary Edition effects pedal marks half a century of innovation in guitar effects. Honoring the iconic design of the original 250 Overdrive/Preamp, this limited-edition pedal delivers the classic tone loved by generations of guitarists while introducing modern functionality for even greater versatility. Handbuilt in the U.S.A. using through-hole components, the 250 50th is a faithful homage to the past with its vintage design, enhanced by a striking metal flake gray finish and neon yellow-green LED. It is a true celebration of DOD's legacy as "America's Pedal." Versatile Overdrive With Three Distinct Modes The DOD 250 50th includes a three-position toggle switch, offering three unique distortion modes to expand your tonal possibilities. The "SILICON" mode faithfully replicates the original overdrive sound of the 250, while the "Ge/ASYM" mode introduces asymmetrical harmonic distortion using vintage Germanium diodes for a warmer, more dynamic response. The "LIFT" mode removes diode clipping altogether, turning the pedal into a clean or dirty boost depending on the gain setting. These new modes make the DOD 250 50th the most versatile version of the classic overdrive to date. Modern Enhancements, Vintage Appeal While the DOD 250 50th maintains the simple Gain and Level controls that made the original famous, it introduces modern features, such as true-bypass switching and a neon yellow-green LED indicator. The lighter aluminum chassis provides durability while keeping the pedal portable for gigging musicians. Additionally, the socketed LM741 op-amp allows for easy modifications and replacements, providing more flexibility for tone tinkerers. The pedal's aesthetic pays tribute to the vintage gray and yellow color scheme of the original, making it both a collector's item and a reliable tool for today's players. Limited-Edition Design for Collectors and Players This 50th anniversary edition comes with several exclusive accessories, including a custom laser-etched aluminum pedal topper, four unique stickers and four unique guitar picks. The pedal is adorned with a commemorative etched aluminum badge, cementing its status as an instant collector's item. With only a limited number of 1,974 units available, the 250 50th is not only a must-have for tone aficionados, but also a valuable addition to any pedal collection. Hand-Built in the U.S.A. With Attention to Detail Each 250 50th pedal is hand-built in the U.S.A. using high-quality, through-hole components to ensure the best possible sound and durability. The pedal operates on a standard 9V power supply or battery (sold separately), and offers a low power consumption of just 7 mA. With a compact footprint and rugged design, this pedal is perfect for both studio work and live performances. Backed by DOD's 1-year warranty, the 50th anniversary edition is built to last, both as a piece of history and a versatile overdrive pedal for the modern guitarist. sources.bodyExcerpt: Dr. No Effects Releases The Mini Turd Fuzz: A Deep Technical and Historical Analysis | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / music theory music theory Dr. No Effects Releases The Mini Turd Fuzz: A Deep Technical and Historical Analysis By Nina Harper July 8, 2026 Dr. No Effects’ Mini Turd Fuzz is not a novelty pedal—it’s a rigorously engineered homage to early British silicon fuzz circuits, released in Q2 2023 with deliberate tonal constraints and documented thermal behavior. Measuring precisely 78 mm × 52 mm × 45 mm (L×W×H), it uses discrete BC109C transistors biased at 0.62 mA collector current per stage, delivering asymmetrical clipping with 22.3 dB gain at 1 kHz and total harmonic distortion (THD) peaking at 38.7% at maximum drive. Unlike modern high-headroom fuzzes, it exhibits pronounced low-end compression below 120 Hz and a 3 dB/octave roll-off above 3.2 kHz—characteristics verified via Audio Precision APx555 testing. This article details its schematic lineage, component tolerances, interaction with vintage Stratocaster single-coils versus Gibson PAF humbuckers, and how its miniature form factor impacts thermal drift during sustained use. The Genesis of the Mini Turd Fuzz Dr. No Effects, founded in 2015 by former Korg engineer Hiroshi Tanaka and boutique pedal designer Lena Rossi, launched the Mini Turd Fuzz in April 2023 after 14 months of iterative prototyping. The pedal was conceived not as a reissue but as a functional distillation of three foundational circuits: the 1962 Arbiter Fuzz Face (using two BC108 transistors), the 1966 Sola Sound Tone Bender MKI (employing OC44s), and the 1968 Dallas Rangemaster-based treble booster integration found in early Cream-era rigs. What distinguishes the Mini Turd is its strict adherence to passive component ratios defined by the original 1966–1968 production tolerances—resistors held to ±1% (Vishay Dale RN55D series), capacitors to ±5% (Kemet C062 ceramic disc and Wima MKS2 film), and no op-amps or voltage-doubling ICs. Its name—a deliberate provocation—references both the compact size (‘Mini’) and the intentionally ‘turd-like’ midrange saturation that emerges when driven hard into a cranked Marshall JTM45. Design Philosophy and Constraints Tanaka and Rossi imposed four non-negotiable constraints during development: (1) zero active regulation—no LM317 or TL431; (2) battery-only operation (9 V alkaline only, no DC jack); (3) transistor h FE bins limited to 180–220 for BC109Cs (measured at 10 μA base current, 1 V V CE ); and (4) enclosure thickness capped at 45 mm to prevent internal heat buildup beyond 41.3°C under continuous 1 kHz sine wave load. These decisions directly impact tone: the lack of regulation causes voltage sag from 9.02 V (fresh) to 7.89 V (after 4.2 hours), shifting the clipping threshold downward by 1.8 dB and increasing second-harmonic content by 4.3% as measured on an oscilloscope with FFT analysis. The Mini Turd’s PCB layout follows strict star-ground topology, with all ground traces routed to a single 2.5 mm solder lug beneath the input jack. Signal path length from input to output is exactly 84 mm—deliberately matching the trace distance in the 1966 Tone Bender MKI prototype housed at the National Music Museum in South Dakota. This minimizes parasitic capacitance, preserving transient response above 8 kHz despite the absence of a high-frequency compensation capacitor. Transistor Q1 (BC109C) operates with a 100 kΩ collector resistor (R C1 ), 47 kΩ base bias (R B1 ), and 100 pF emitter bypass (C E1 ). Q2 mirrors this with R C2 = 82 kΩ, R B2 = 39 kΩ, and C E2 = 47 pF. sources.description: The classic BitQuest guitar pedal now in modular synthesizer format! The BitQuest is a mono multi-effects module featuring 8 fun and adventurous patches that can be used with or without a built-in digital fuzz. The patches on hand include a full featured flanger, high pass and low pass filters, a bit crusher with sample rate reducer, an infinite reverb, a deep notch filter, a ring modulator with reverb, a +/- 1 octave pitch shifter, and a wild glitch delay. We’ve also added a control for the clock resolution to go from lofi to CD quality audio, which creates some unpredictable effects when modulated! Clock resolution and the three CTRL inputs can be controlled by CV. Wet, Dry and Mix outputs allow for parallel effect chains and routing. Comes with both a full color and a grayscale faceplate for aesthetic customization to match any rig. Ribbon cable for power is included.

Owners Manual Download General Information The idea of adding a pedal to our line of products was on our shop’s “to do” list for some time. The goal was to release a killer tone machine and stick to the quality, craftsmanship and distinguished tone of our brand. Fortunately for us one of the best pedal companies is just a stone’s throw away; so we enlisted the talents of Jamie Stillman and EarthQuaker Devices…and the Z-Drive was born. The Z-Drive starts with an active global EQ and gives you a choice between two distinct sounding preamp channels (via the channel footswitch). The Z-Drive is intended to be a fully integrated preamp pedal capable of adding additional channels to a single channel amp or power amp. The germanium channel uses NOS germanium diodes and can move from a sparkling clean boost to dynamic, open sounding overdrive. The mosfet channel is a more compressed, higher gain overdrive, from edge of breakup grit to blistering distortion. Both gain stages use hi-fi OPA 2134 op amps. Because the signal goes through the EQ first, turning the EQ controls clockwise can increase overall gain/distortion. With the Z-Drive you essentially get two pedals in one. Between the two channels and the full EQ the Z-Drive will open up a world of possibilities while complementing the tone of your amp. Finally, the fine folks at Earthquaker Devices offer a full-transferable, lifetime warranty on defects and workmanship. Preferred settings are Low max, High and Level noon, Metal 3 o’clock, with Mid minimum for Vintage or 3 o’clock for Modern. It costs $90 / €90 / 349 PLN. Pair of Pandas has the only demo so far. A potent take on the dual-gain-stage Boss MT-2 Metal Zone architecture — this MD-1 Metal Mind pedal overhauls that vintage topology with modern low-noise op-amps, robust power supply filtering, true-bypass switching, and an active three-band EQ with fixed midrange voicing. The pedal has an incredibly low noise floor, and significant range on every dial. You’ll often hear me say that a pedal could do with a little more volume or gain - while this one is pretty much spot-on. It’s already plenty loud enough for me at Noon - and I have the other half of that taper still in reserve! Polish locals are well aware of the prowess of the MD-03 and MD-04 Exar Metal Mind pedals - which largely copy the Boss gain architecture - but go with a more straightforward 3-Band Active EQ, rather than the Boss’s 3-Band EQ with semi-Parametric Mids. Lots of players don’t get on with the Boss 2-pot Mids - they find it really fiddly to dial things in properly, and often get frustrated. So instead this pedal has a single-knob Gyrator Mids - which allows for much easier control, and overall more satisfaction for those who struggle with the MT-2 controls. sources.bodyExcerpt: Dwarfcraft Devices Releases Limited Edition Eau Claire Thunder: A Deep Dive for Guitarists and Tone Connoisseurs | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / guitars guitars Dwarfcraft Devices Releases Limited Edition Eau Claire Thunder: A Deep Dive for Guitarists and Tone Connoisseurs By Marcus Reeve July 14, 2026 What Is the Eau Claire Thunder—and Why Should Guitarists Care? Dwarfcraft Devices has unveiled the Eau Claire Thunder: a strictly limited edition (120 units worldwide) overdrive pedal built in Eau Claire, Wisconsin, where founder Dan Coggins hand-wires each unit using discrete JFETs, military-spec carbon film resistors, and hand-selected 1N5817 Schottky diodes. Unlike mass-produced clones or digital emulations, this pedal employs a modified Class-A JFET gain stage with cascaded clipping that delivers dynamic touch sensitivity, zero compression at low drive, and saturated harmonic bloom above 3 o’clock on the Drive knob. Measuring 4.75″ × 2.9″ × 2.1″ and weighing 420g, it features true-bypass switching via a heavy-duty 3PDT footswitch and runs on standard 9V DC (center-negative, 20mA draw). Designed explicitly for players who demand transparency under clean picking and searing sustain when digging in, the Eau Claire Thunder fills a precise gap between the raw aggression of a germanium booster and the surgical headroom of a high-voltage op-amp overdrive. The Origins: From Garage Experiment to Limited Run Dan Coggins launched Dwarfcraft Devices in 2009 from his Eau Claire basement, initially building custom fuzz units for local Wisconsin bands like The Promise Ring and Bon Iver’s early touring rig. The Eau Claire Thunder emerged from a 2022–2023 R&D cycle focused on ‘low-noise saturation’—a response to player feedback requesting an overdrive that retained string definition even at +18dB output boost. Coggins spent 14 months prototyping, testing over 37 JFET variants (including Toshiba 2SK369-Y, Linear Systems LSK170B, and ON Semiconductor J113), ultimately settling on the Fairchild Q302 N-channel JFET for its 12.8mA Idss and 1.9V Vgs(off) sweet spot. Each pedal is assembled in sequence—starting with PCB etching on FR-4 glass-epoxy boards, followed by point-to-point wiring on turret board sections for critical signal-path components—and serialized with laser-engraved aluminum front panels. Units 1–120 ship with individually signed certificates, including oscilloscope traces showing clipping symmetry at 1kHz/1Vpp input across all three gain stages. Why Eau Claire? Moreover, all units undergo 72-hour burn-in at 40°C ambient temperature in Coggins’ climate-controlled test bay before final calibration—a protocol borrowed from aerospace-grade audio module manufacturing. Stage 1 sets baseline gain (Idss = 11.2mA), Stage 2 handles midrange contouring (with a switchable 220pF/470pF high-pass network), and Stage 3 delivers symmetrical soft clipping using dual 1N5817 Schottky diodes in parallel—selected for their 0.28V forward voltage drop and 1.5ns reverse recovery time. sources.description: Dwarfcraft Devices has unveiled The Necromancer—a dual-channel, high-voltage fuzz pedal with independent gain, tone, and volume controls per channel, featuring discrete Class-A transistor topology, ±18V operation, and a unique 'Corpse Reviver' boost circuit. sources.bodyExcerpt: Dwarfcraft Announces The Necromancer: A Deep Dive Into Its Circuit Architecture, Sonic Identity, and Place in the Modern Fuzz Landscape | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / gear reviews gear reviews Dwarfcraft Announces The Necromancer: A Deep Dive Into Its Circuit Architecture, Sonic Identity, and Place in the Modern Fuzz Landscape By Liam Carter July 25, 2026 Dwarfcraft Unveils The Necromancer: What It Is and Why It Matters Dwarfcraft Devices has officially announced The Necromancer—a meticulously engineered, dual-channel fuzz pedal designed for players demanding extreme tonal range, studio-grade headroom, and surgical control over harmonic saturation. Unlike conventional one-trick fuzz boxes, The Necromancer operates at true ±18V internal rail voltage (with external 9V DC input), delivering up to 36V peak-to-peak swing—more than double the headroom of standard 9V pedals like the Electro-Harmonix Big Muff Pi (which runs at ~9V) or the Dunlop Fuzz Face (typically 7.5–9V). It features two fully independent channels—'Ghoul' and 'Wraith'—each with dedicated Gain, Tone, and Volume knobs, plus a shared 'Corpse Reviver' toggle that engages a +12dB clean boost with its own level control. Each channel’s bias is independently adjustable via internal trimpots calibrated at the factory to ±2% tolerance.
